title: Transactions & Isolation
subtitle: Watch two concurrent transactions corrupt a bank balance, then see how logs, row versions, and locks stop it.
learn: What each letter of ACID promises, and which part of the engine delivers it
How lost updates, dirty reads, and write skew actually happen
How MVCC lets readers and writers work without blocking each other
When to reach for row locks, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or serializable isolation
Why stronger isolation costs waiting or retries

steps.title: Two people, one balance
steps.body: An account holds $100. Transaction A and Transaction B each try to withdraw $30 at the same moment, perhaps from two phones. The right final balance is $40. A database serving thousands of requests per second must get this right every time, even when requests overlap or the machine dies halfway. The tool for this is the transaction: a group of reads and writes treated as one unit.
steps.idea: A transaction groups operations into one all-or-nothing unit, and the database must stop overlapping units from corrupting each other.
steps.caption: Two transactions are about to touch the same $100 account row.

steps.title: All or nothing
steps.body: A withdrawal debits the account and also writes an audit row. If the server crashes between the two writes, money is gone with no record. Atomicity means both writes happen or neither does. In the animation, A's two writes go to the transaction manager, which first appends them to a write-ahead log (WAL), a sequential file tagged with the transaction id. After a crash the engine replays or undoes work from that log, so a half-finished transaction never survives a restart.
steps.idea: Atomicity comes from logging changes first, so an unfinished transaction can always be rolled back.
steps.caption: A's two writes are logged before they count.

steps.title: Commit means it stays
steps.body: A withdraws $30, so the balance becomes 70. When A sends COMMIT, the engine forces the log onto disk (an fsync) and only then answers 'committed'. On datacenter NVMe with power-loss protection an fsync is often 0.1-1 ms; on a network cloud disk, roughly 1-5 ms or more (rule of thumb). That is durability: a committed transaction survives a power cut. Consistency, the C in ACID, means your rules (no negative balance, foreign keys) hold before and after. The database enforces declared constraints; your code defines the rest.
steps.idea: Durability means the commit record is on disk before the client hears 'committed'.
steps.caption: The commit waits for the log to reach disk, then A is told it succeeded.

steps.title: Lost update
steps.body: The balance is reset to $100. Each anomaly in this lesson (a wrong result caused by overlapping transactions) is its own scenario. Here A and B overlap. Both read the balance (100) into the application, subtract 30 in code, and write back 70. A writes 70, then B writes 70. Each looked fine alone, but one withdrawal vanished: the balance should be 40. This is a lost update, the classic bug of doing read, change, write in application code without protection.
steps.idea: A lost update happens when two transactions read the same old value and the later write overwrites the earlier one.
steps.caption: Both read 100 and both write 70, so one withdrawal is lost.

steps.title: Dirty read
steps.body: New scenario, balance back at $100. A writes 70 but has not committed yet. Imagine a database that lets B read that uncommitted 70 and act on it. If A then rolls back, B used a number that never officially existed. That is a dirty read. The Read Committed isolation level (the default in PostgreSQL and many others) forbids it: you only see data from transactions that have committed. Isolation levels are settings that say which anomalies you may see.
steps.idea: Isolation levels promise which anomalies you will never see; Read Committed rules out dirty reads.
steps.caption: B reads A's uncommitted write, then A rolls back. Read Committed prevents this.

steps.title: Keep old versions around
steps.body: Instead of blocking readers while A writes, most modern engines (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle) use multi-version concurrency control, or MVCC. A write creates a new version of the row and keeps the old one, so the table now has 2 versions. Each transaction reads from a snapshot, a frozen view of the data, so B keeps seeing 100 until A commits. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers. The price is storage for old versions and cleanup later (VACUUM in PostgreSQL).
steps.idea: MVCC gives each transaction a consistent snapshot by keeping old row versions, so reads do not wait for writes.
steps.caption: A creates version v2 (70). B still reads the old version v1 (100).

steps.title: Make B wait its turn
steps.body: Snapshots stop dirty reads but not lost updates in app code. The fix is to lock the row you plan to change: SELECT balance FROM accounts WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE. A gets the row lock first. B asks for the same lock and must wait. After A commits, B's read returns 70 and B writes 40. B waited about 12 ms, but the answer is correct. If A and B each hold one lock and wait for the other's, that is a deadlock; the database aborts one and the app must retry. Often one statement is enough: UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 30.
steps.idea: Row locks make writers on the same row take turns: you buy correctness with waiting.
steps.caption: B waits on A's row lock, then sees 70 and writes 40.

steps.title: Write skew
steps.body: Locking only the row you write does not help when two transactions write different rows based on a shared rule. Reset: checking and savings hold $60 each, and the rule is that the total must stay at or above 0. A withdraws $100 from checking, B withdraws $100 from savings. Each checks the total (120), sees room, and writes a different row. Snapshot isolation (one snapshot for the whole transaction, called Repeatable Read in PostgreSQL) sees no write conflict, so both commit and the total becomes -80. Fix: use Serializable, or lock every row the check reads.
steps.idea: Write skew breaks a rule that spans several rows even though no single row was written twice.
steps.caption: Different rows, one shared rule: both commit and the total drops to -80.

steps.title: Serializable and its price
steps.body: Serializable isolation promises results as if transactions ran one at a time. PostgreSQL tracks what each transaction read and wrote. On a dangerous pattern it aborts one with a serialization error, and the app must retry. It may abort some transactions that would have been fine. The ladder: Read Committed blocks dirty reads. Repeatable Read (snapshot) adds a stable view but still allows write skew. Serializable also blocks write skew. Safety and cost rise together, so protect only risky paths.
steps.idea: Stronger isolation trades throughput for safety: more waiting, or more aborted transactions to retry.
steps.caption: A commits. B is aborted, retries, sees total 20, and refuses the $100 withdrawal.

steps.title: Pick the weakest safe tool
steps.body: ACID in one line each: atomic via the log, consistent via your rules, isolated via MVCC and locks, durable via fsync on commit. For lost updates use an atomic UPDATE or FOR UPDATE. Dirty reads are gone at Read Committed. Write skew needs Serializable, or locking every row the check reads. Keep transactions short, retry on serialization or deadlock errors, and never hold one open while waiting for a user click. Transactions across several databases need more machinery, covered later.
steps.idea: Use the cheapest mechanism that rules out the anomaly you actually risk, and always be ready to retry.
steps.caption: The log, row versions, and locks each cover a different failure.

quiz.q: Two requests each run SELECT balance, compute balance - 30 in app code, then UPDATE with the computed value. Both read 100. What final balance results at Read Committed with no locks?
options: 100, because both transactions roll back
40, because the database serializes the updates
The second transaction always gets an error
70, because the second write overwrites the first
quiz.why: Read Committed does not stop two transactions reading the same old value. The later write of 70 overwrites the earlier one, a lost update.

quiz.q: Why does MVCC let a long report query run while writers keep updating the same table?
options: Writers are paused until the report ends
The report reads a snapshot made of older row versions, so it does not need locks held by writers
The report reads uncommitted data
The report runs on the write-ahead log
quiz.why: MVCC keeps old versions, so the reader sees a consistent snapshot while writers create new versions. Neither blocks the other.

quiz.q: On-call rule: at least one doctor must stay on call. Two doctors, both on call, each check the count (2) and then set only their own row to off. Both commit under snapshot isolation. What happened?
options: A dirty read
A lost update
Write skew
A deadlock
quiz.why: They wrote different rows, so there was no write-write conflict, yet the shared rule broke. That is write skew, prevented by Serializable or a lock on a shared row.

quiz.q: Your service runs at Serializable isolation and sometimes gets a serialization error on commit. What is the correct response?
options: Rerun the whole transaction from the start, usually with a small retry limit
Treat it as a bug and lower the isolation level silently
Ignore it, the data is already saved
Retry only the last statement
quiz.why: A serialization failure means the transaction was aborted to keep results correct. The whole transaction must be retried, since its earlier reads may now be stale.

quiz.q: What does the write-ahead log mainly provide?
options: Faster reads through caching
Atomic rollback and durable commits after a crash
Protection against write skew
Automatic sharding
quiz.why: Logging changes before applying them lets the engine undo unfinished transactions and replay committed ones after a crash.

cheatsheet.def: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (rules hold), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed data survives crashes).
Reading another transaction's uncommitted data, which may later be rolled back. Prevented from Read Committed upward.
Two read-modify-write cycles overlap and one overwrites the other. Fix with atomic UPDATE, SELECT FOR UPDATE, or optimistic version checks (UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?).
Two transactions read overlapping data, write different rows, and together break a rule. Needs Serializable or an explicit shared lock.
Multi-version concurrency control: writes add row versions and reads use snapshots, so readers and writers rarely block each other.
Read Committed (PostgreSQL default): no dirty reads. Repeatable Read/snapshot (MySQL default): stable view, still allows write skew. Serializable: blocks all three. Engines vary.
Reads rows and locks them until commit, so concurrent writers wait. Keep the transaction short to limit waiting and deadlocks.
Serialization failures and deadlocks are normal under contention. Rerun the whole transaction, with a cap and a little jitter.
